scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Madison was created and first danced in Columbus, Ohio, in 1957.
It gained local popularity before spreading nationally in 1960 when The Buddy Deane Show in Baltimore featured it.
The dance inspired teams, competitions, and many recordings during the late 1950s and early 1960s.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social novelty dance popular in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the Madison was danced on television and at social gatherings.
It remains popular in Cambodia at weddings and parties, where it is performed in large groups.
The dance is associated with nostalgia for the early 1960s in the US and is featured in films and musicals like Hairspray.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Madison is a line dance performed without partner contact, typically in lines or multiple rows.

The basic step sequence includes stepping left forward, placing the right foot beside the left with a clap, stepping back on the right, moving the left foot back and across the right, then moving the left foot to the left and back across the right again.
Called steps add named sequences like the Double Cross and Jackie Gleason, which dancers perform on cue.
Watch for Double Cross, Jackie Gleason, Cleveland Box.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers arranged side by side in lines or multiple rows, maintaining personal space without contact

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Madison music is typically slow to medium tempo 4/4 rhythm, around 30 to 44 beats per minute.
Key recordings include "Madison Time" by Ray Bryant (1959) and "The Madison" by Al Brown & The Tunetoppers (1960), which feature clear vocal calls for the dance steps.
Listen for the jazz piano, brass, rhythm section.
The pulse is 4/4.
The music features a steady 4/4 beat with jazz piano and brass accents, punctuated by vocal calls that cue dancers through the step sequences, creating an engaging and participatory atmosphere.

The Madison is danced mainly as a line dance in the US and France, with couple versions existing but less common.
The Madison is a novelty line dance from the late 1950s US, influenced by earlier social dances like the Twist.
